c: 19-year-old with dull pain around the belly button since this morning.
The pain has moved to the lower right belly. Nauseous, doesn't want to eat.
Temp 100.8°F, heart rate 104.
Tender at McBurney's point, pain when the hand is released (rebound), and pressing the LEFT side hurts the right (Rovsing sign).
White blood cells 15,000 with a left shift.
CT: swollen 9 mm appendix with fat stranding around it.
rounds.rev: The appendix gets blocked (hard stool or swollen lymph tissue), swells, loses blood supply and bacteria invade. Pain starts vague at the belly button (gut nerves, T10) then moves to the right lower belly when the lining (parietal peritoneum) gets irritated. Treatment: laparoscopic appendectomy + IV antibiotics; some simple cases are treated with antibiotics alone.

c: 44-year-old woman, upper belly pain that started about an hour after a big burger-and-fries dinner.
Pain settles in the upper RIGHT, steady for more than 6 hours, spreads to the right shoulder blade. Vomited once.
Temp 101.2°F, heart rate 98.
Murphy's sign: she stops breathing in when the doctor presses under the right ribs.
White cells 14,000; liver tests mostly normal.
Ultrasound: gallstones, thick gallbladder wall, fluid around it.
rounds.rev: A gallstone blocks the cystic duct, bile sits trapped, the wall inflames and can get infected. Compared with biliary colic, it lasts more than 6 hours and comes with fever. Treatment: nothing by mouth, IV fluids, antibiotics, then laparoscopic cholecystectomy, usually within 72 hours.

c: 52-year-old man, severe upper-middle belly pain boring straight through to his back since this morning.
Leaning forward helps, lying flat makes it worse. Vomiting a lot.
He has been a heavy drinker for years.
Heart rate 118, BP 100/60, temp 100.9°F, tender upper belly.
Lipase more than 3 times the upper limit of normal.
CT: swollen pancreas with fat stranding around it.
rounds.rev: Digestive enzymes (trypsin) switch on inside the pancreas and start digesting it. Top two causes: gallstones and alcohol. Diagnosis needs 2 of 3: typical pain, lipase over 3× normal, imaging. Treatment: lots of IV fluids, pain control, early feeding, stop alcohol; ERCP if a stone is stuck with infection; remove the gallbladder if gallstones caused it.

c: 35-year-old man, burning upper-middle belly pain for weeks. It gets BETTER right after eating, worse 2–3 hours later and at night.
He takes ibuprofen every day for back pain.
Dark, tarry poop (melena) this week.
Blood test: mild anaemia (low haemoglobin).
Breath / stool test positive for H. pylori.
Endoscopy: a crater in the first part of the small intestine (duodenum).
rounds.rev: Acid and pepsin eat through the lining when its defences drop. H. pylori bacteria and NSAIDs (which block the protective COX-1 prostaglandins) are the top causes. Barry Marshall drank a flask of H. pylori in 1984 to prove it, and won the Nobel Prize in 2005. Treatment: stop the NSAID, proton pump inhibitor + antibiotics to clear H. pylori.
rounds.res: Solved-ish: you gave the right plan without the name

c: 60-year-old woman, crampy belly pain coming in WAVES, vomiting, belly getting swollen.
She had belly surgery 10 years ago.
No poop and no gas for 2 days.
High-pitched tinkling bowel sounds, belly drum-tight.
X-ray: stacked, swollen loops of bowel with air-fluid levels (stepladder pattern).
Scar tissue inside the belly is the cause.
rounds.rev: Adhesions (scar tissue from old surgery) are the #1 cause, then hernias and tumours. The gut keeps squeezing against the blockage, so the pain comes in waves. Danger: strangulation (blood supply cut off → dead bowel). CT confirms it. Treatment: 'drip and suck' (nothing by mouth, a tube through the nose to empty the stomach, IV fluids), surgery if strangulated or not improving.
rounds.res: Abandoned that night; solved on guess 1 the next day

c: 45-year-old woman, sudden severe upper-middle pain boring to the back, vomiting.
She does NOT drink alcohol at all.
For months she's had right-upper pain after fatty meals.
Lipase 5 times normal.
Ultrasound: gallstones and a widened bile duct.
Her eyes are turning yellow.
rounds.rev: A gallstone gets stuck where the bile duct and pancreatic duct meet (the ampulla), so pancreatic enzymes back up. Treatment: fluids, pain control, early feeding; ERCP to pull the stone if the bile duct is infected; remove the gallbladder during the same hospital stay so it doesn't happen again.

c: 38-year-old woman, upper-right belly pain 1 hour after a cheeseburger.
It lasted 2 hours, then went away completely.
No fever, heart rate 80.
Murphy's sign negative now.
Ultrasound: gallstones, but a normal gallbladder wall and normal ducts.
It's happened 3 times this year.
rounds.rev: A stone briefly plugs the cystic duct, the gallbladder squeezes against it, then it unplugs and the pain stops. No inflammation, no fever (that would be cholecystitis). Treatment: planned laparoscopic gallbladder removal; low-fat food until then.

c: 29-year-old woman, sudden sharp chest pain that's worse when she breathes in, plus short of breath.
She got off a 14-hour flight from Tokyo 2 days ago.
Her mum and uncle have both had blood clots.
Heart rate 118, oxygen 91%, her right calf is swollen and tender.
ECG: sinus tachycardia. Troponin normal, D-dimer high.
CT angiogram: a clot in the pulmonary artery.
rounds.rev: A deep vein clot (DVT) breaks off and lodges in the lung arteries. Long trips, immobility, surgery and clotting tendencies raise the risk (Virchow's triad: slow flow, vessel damage, sticky blood). Treatment: anticoagulants (heparin, then a DOAC); clot-busting drugs if she's in shock.

c: Severe upper belly pain boring straight through to the back.
Nausea and vomiting; leaning forward helps.
Heavy drinker; big binge last night.
Tender upper belly, fast heart rate, low fever.
Lipase more than 3× normal.
CT: swollen, inflamed pancreas.
rounds.rev: Alcohol triggers early enzyme activation inside the pancreas. Lipase first; CT only if the diagnosis is unclear or complications are suspected. Treatment: IV fluids, pain control, early feeding, stop alcohol.

c: 30-year-old man with sudden, severe pain in his left flank, coming in waves.
Can't sit still, keeps pacing and curling up.
Pain spreads down toward the groin.
No fever.
Urine dipstick: blood.
CT without contrast: a 5 mm stone in the left ureter.
rounds.rev: Crystals (usually calcium oxalate) form a stone that gets stuck in the ureter; the ureter spasms around it, causing waves of pain. Small stones usually pass with pain relief (NSAIDs) and fluids; alpha-blockers help them pass. Big or infected ones need a stent or lithotripsy.

c: 17-year-old, suddenly itchy all over minutes after eating at a new restaurant.
Lips and tongue swelling.
Hoarse voice, wheezing.
Hives all over the body.
BP 82/50, heart rate 130.
He has a known peanut allergy; the sauce had peanuts.
rounds.rev: IgE antibodies on mast cells grab the allergen and trigger a massive histamine release: blood vessels leak and widen (low BP, swelling) and airways tighten. Treatment: intramuscular epinephrine first and fast, then oxygen, IV fluids, antihistamines and steroids; carry an auto-injector after.

c: 58-year-old man, crushing chest pressure for 40 minutes, like an elephant sitting on him.
Pain spreads to his left arm and jaw; sweaty and nauseous.
Smoker, high blood pressure, high cholesterol.
Not affected by position or breathing; calves normal.
ECG: ST elevation in leads II, III and aVF.
Troponin very high.
rounds.rev: A fatty plaque in a coronary artery ruptures and a clot blocks it; heart muscle starts dying within minutes. ST elevation in II, III, aVF = inferior wall (right coronary artery). Treatment: aspirin, antiplatelet, anticoagulant, and emergency stenting (PCI) to open the artery; then beta-blockers, statins, ACE inhibitors.

c: High fever with shaking chills.
Pain in one side of the back / flank.
Burning when peeing and peeing a lot for 3 days before.
Tender when the doctor taps over the kidney (CVA tenderness); nausea and vomiting.
Urine: white cells, nitrites, white cell casts.
Urine culture grows E. coli.
rounds.rev: Bacteria (usually E. coli from the gut) climb from the bladder up the ureter into the kidney. Casts prove it's in the kidney, not just the bladder. Treatment: antibiotics (IV if very unwell); imaging if not improving to look for a blockage or abscess.

c: Sudden sharp one-sided chest pain and short of breath at rest.
Tall, skinny 19-year-old guy, smoker, no injury.
Breath sounds reduced on that side.
That side sounds hollow when tapped (hyperresonant).
Chest X-ray: a thin pleural line with no lung markings beyond it.
Windpipe in the middle and BP fine: NOT a tension pneumothorax.
rounds.rev: Small air blisters (blebs) at the lung tip pop, air leaks into the pleural space and the lung collapses. Tall thin young men and smokers are at risk. Small: oxygen and watch. Big: needle aspiration or chest tube. Keeps coming back: VATS surgery to stick the lung to the chest wall (pleurodesis).

c: Burning chest pain behind the sternum (chest bone) after meals.
Worse lying down and at night; 30-year-old man, coffee and late big dinners, overweight.
Sour taste in the mouth, chronic cough, hoarse in the mornings.
Exam normal; ECG and troponin normal (not a heart attack).
Gets better with antacids and a 2-week PPI trial.
Endoscopy: inflamed lower oesophagus (erosive oesophagitis).
rounds.rev: The lower oesophageal sphincter relaxes when it shouldn't, so stomach acid splashes up. Treatment ladder: lifestyle (no late meals, raise the head of the bed, weight loss), antacids, H2 blockers, proton pump inhibitors; surgery (Nissen fundoplication) if nothing works. Long-term acid damage can cause Barrett's oesophagus.

c: 18-year-old college student with a terrible headache and fever since this morning.
Neck is stiff; bright light hurts his eyes.
Getting confused and drowsy.
Bending his neck makes his knees bend up (Brudzinski sign); a purple rash that doesn't fade when pressed with a glass.
Lumbar puncture: cloudy fluid, lots of neutrophils, high protein, LOW glucose.
Gram stain: gram-negative diplococci (Neisseria meningitidis).
rounds.rev: Bacteria infect the meninges; the body's inflammation raises brain pressure. The non-blanching rash means bloodstream spread (meningococcaemia). Treatment: IV antibiotics immediately (don't wait for the LP if it will be delayed) plus steroids; close contacts get preventive antibiotics. Vaccines prevent most cases.

c: 45-year-old woman, sudden 'worst headache of my life' that peaked within seconds.
It hit while lifting something heavy. She vomited.
Stiff neck, light hurts.
Her left eyelid droops and that pupil is big.
CT head: blood in the spaces around the brain (the cisterns).
CT angiogram: a berry aneurysm on the posterior communicating artery.
rounds.rev: A berry aneurysm in the circle of Willis bursts, bleeding into the subarachnoid space. A big pupil = the aneurysm pressing on CN III. Treatment: secure the aneurysm (endovascular coiling or surgical clipping), nimodipine to prevent vasospasm, manage pressure and hydrocephalus.

c: 16-year-old hit on the side of the head by a baseball.
Knocked out for a few seconds, then woke up and felt fine for an hour.
Now his headache is getting worse and he's getting sleepy.
One pupil is getting bigger; the other side of his body is weak.
Skull X-ray / CT: a fracture of the temporal bone.
CT: lens-shaped bright blood pressed against the skull.
rounds.rev: The temporal bone fracture tears the middle meningeal artery; arterial blood strips the dura off the skull, making a lens shape that can't cross sutures. The 'lucid interval' then decline is classic. It's a neurosurgical emergency: craniotomy to remove the clot.

c: 68-year-old man suddenly can't lift his right arm, started 40 minutes ago.
Right side of the face droops; words come out jumbled.
Has atrial fibrillation and stopped his blood thinner.
BP 180/100. Blood sugar normal.
CT head: no bleeding.
CT angiogram: a clot blocking the left middle cerebral artery.
rounds.rev: A clot (here from the heart in AF) blocks a brain artery and the brain tissue starts dying ('time is brain'). Left MCA = right-sided weakness + speech problems. Treatment: clot-busting drug (thrombolysis) if within the time window and no bleed, plus mechanical thrombectomy for big vessel clots; then anticoagulation for AF.

c: 26-year-old woman, blurry vision in her right eye that hurts when she moves it.
It got better over a few weeks on its own.
A year later: numbness and tingling in both legs for a week.
An electric shock down her spine when she bends her neck (Lhermitte sign).
Lumbar puncture: oligoclonal bands.
MRI: bright white-matter patches around the ventricles (Dawson's fingers).
rounds.rev: The immune system attacks myelin in the brain and spinal cord, in episodes separated in time and space. Optic neuritis is a common first episode. Treatment: steroids for attacks; disease-modifying drugs (e.g. interferons, monoclonal antibodies) to prevent new ones.

c: 66-year-old man whose right hand shakes when it's resting in his lap.
The shake goes away when he reaches for something.
His handwriting has got tiny; his face looks less expressive.
Walks with small shuffling steps, arms don't swing; stiff 'cogwheel' feel when the doctor moves his wrist.
He's had no sense of smell for years and acts out his dreams.
DaT scan: reduced dopamine uptake in the striatum.
rounds.rev: Dopamine neurons in the substantia nigra die, so the basal ganglia circuits can't start movements smoothly: tremor at rest, rigidity, slowness. Treatment: levodopa with carbidopa, dopamine agonists, MAO-B inhibitors; deep brain stimulation for advanced cases.

c: 15-year-old suddenly cried out and fell to the floor in class.
Whole body went stiff, then jerked rhythmically for 2 minutes.
Bit the side of his tongue and wet himself.
Afterwards very confused and sleepy for 30 minutes.
Had stayed up all night gaming before it happened.
EEG: generalised spike-and-wave discharges.
rounds.rev: A burst of abnormal synchronised electrical activity across both hemispheres. Sleep deprivation and flashing lights can trigger it. A side-of-tongue bite and long confusion after point to a seizure rather than a faint. Treatment: protect from injury during the seizure; a benzodiazepine if it lasts over 5 minutes; antiseizure medicines (e.g. levetiracetam, valproate) for epilepsy.

c: 15-year-old football player took a helmet-to-helmet hit.
Didn't black out but felt 'foggy' and dazed.
Headache, dizzy, light and noise bother him.
Can't remember the play right before the hit.
Neuro exam normal; balance a bit off.
CT not needed; it would be normal.
rounds.rev: A rapid shake of the brain causes a temporary energy crisis in neurons rather than a structural injury, so scans are normal. Treatment: off the field the same day, relative rest for a day or two, then a graded return to school and sport. A second hit before recovery is dangerous.

c: 14-year-old with belly pain and vomiting since yesterday.
For weeks: always thirsty, peeing all the time, lost weight without trying.
Breathing deep and fast; his breath smells fruity.
Dry mouth, heart rate 125.
Glucose very high, ketones in blood, pH 7.12, low bicarbonate.
Potassium normal now but will drop with treatment.
rounds.rev: No insulin (new type 1 diabetes) means cells can't use glucose, so fat is burned into acidic ketones. Deep fast breathing (Kussmaul) blows off CO₂ to fight the acid. Treatment: IV fluids, insulin infusion, potassium replacement, find the trigger.

c: 24-year-old woman who feels hot and sweaty all the time.
Lost weight while eating more; anxious, can't sleep.
Heart races; hands shake.
Eyes look like they're bulging; a smooth swelling in the front of the neck.
TSH very low, free T4 high.
TSH-receptor antibodies positive.
rounds.rev: Antibodies switch on the TSH receptor, so the thyroid overproduces hormone. The same immune process swells the tissue behind the eyes. Treatment: beta-blockers for symptoms, antithyroid drugs (methimazole), radioactive iodine or surgery.

c: 15-year-old who's tired all the time and gets breathless climbing stairs.
Vegetarian; doesn't eat many iron-rich foods.
Craves ice and chews it constantly (pica).
Pale inner eyelids, spoon-shaped nails.
Haemoglobin low, small pale red cells (low MCV).
Ferritin very low.
rounds.rev: Not enough iron to make haemoglobin, so red cells come out small and pale. Ferritin is the iron store test. Treatment: iron supplements and diet, and look for blood loss (gut) in adults.

c: 13-year-old with severe pain in his back, arms and legs.
It started after a cold, dehydrated football practice.
He's had episodes like this since he was little.
Mildly yellow eyes; spleen not felt.
Haemoglobin low; blood film shows crescent-shaped cells.
Haemoglobin electrophoresis: HbSS.
rounds.rev: A single amino acid change in haemoglobin makes it stick together when oxygen is low, so red cells bend into sickles that block small vessels (painful crisis) and break apart (anaemia, jaundice). Treatment: pain relief, fluids, oxygen if low; hydroxyurea prevents crises; watch for acute chest syndrome.

c: 70-year-old with cough and fever for 3 days.
Coughing up rusty-coloured phlegm; sharp pain on the right when he breathes in.
Temp 102°F, breathing 26/min, oxygen 90%.
Crackles and bronchial breathing at the right base.
White cells 18,000, CRP high.
Chest X-ray: white patch filling the right lower lobe.
rounds.rev: Bacteria (most often Streptococcus pneumoniae) fill the air sacs with pus, so that part of the lung can't swap oxygen. Severity scores (like CURB-65) decide home vs hospital. Treatment: antibiotics, oxygen, fluids.

c: 50-year-old man woke up with his big toe red, hot and so painful a bedsheet hurts.
Steak dinner and lots of beer last night.
Takes a water pill (diuretic) for blood pressure.
Big toe joint swollen and shiny.
Uric acid high (can be normal during an attack).
Joint fluid: needle-shaped crystals that are negatively birefringent.
rounds.rev: Uric acid crystallises in the joint and triggers intense inflammation. Purines (red meat, beer) and diuretics raise uric acid. Treatment for an attack: NSAIDs, colchicine or steroids; long-term: allopurinol to lower uric acid.

c: 14-year-old with bloating and loose, greasy, smelly poop for months.
Lost weight; shorter than his classmates.
Tired; blood tests show low iron.
Itchy blistering rash on his elbows (dermatitis herpetiformis).
Tissue transglutaminase (tTG) antibodies high.
Small-bowel biopsy: flattened villi.
rounds.rev: Gluten triggers an immune attack on the small intestine lining, flattening the villi so nutrients aren't absorbed. Treatment: strict lifelong gluten-free diet, after which the gut heals.

c: 3-year-old with a fever over 102°F for 6 days.
Both eyes red but no discharge.
Red cracked lips and a 'strawberry' tongue.
Swollen, red hands and feet, then skin peeling from the fingertips; a big neck lymph node.
CRP and platelets high.
Echocardiogram: widened coronary arteries.
rounds.rev: A childhood inflammation of medium blood vessels; the danger is coronary artery aneurysms. Treatment: IV immunoglobulin and aspirin (one of the few times aspirin is given to children), then heart follow-up.

c: 40-year-old with a red, hot, swollen patch on his lower leg for 2 days.
It started near a scratch from gardening.
The red edge is spreading; he drew around it and it's grown.
Fever 100.9°F.
White cells raised.
No pus pocket on ultrasound (not an abscess).
rounds.rev: Bacteria (Streptococcus or Staphylococcus) get under the skin through a break and spread in the deeper layers. Treatment: antibiotics, raise the leg, mark the edges to track it; drain any abscess.

c: 17-year-old collapses at the end of a summer football practice.
Confused and talking nonsense.
Core temperature 105.8°F.
Skin hot; heart rate 140, BP low.
Kidney and liver tests rising; muscle enzyme (CK) high.
It's 98°F and humid; he skipped water breaks.
rounds.rev: The body's cooling fails, core temperature rises over 104°F and brain, liver, kidney and muscle cells start breaking down. Confusion separates heat stroke from heat exhaustion. Treatment: cool first, transport second (cold-water immersion), then fluids and organ support.

c: 35-year-old woman who's always cold and tired.
Gained weight without eating more; constipated.
Dry skin, thinning hair, feels slowed down.
Slow pulse; reflexes relax slowly.
TSH high, free T4 low.
Anti-TPO antibodies positive.
rounds.rev: The immune system slowly destroys the thyroid, so less hormone is made and the pituitary pumps out more TSH trying to push it. Treatment: daily levothyroxine (synthetic T4), adjusted by TSH.

c: 20-year-old had food poisoning with diarrhoea 2 weeks ago.
Now tingling in his feet, and his legs feel weak.
Over 3 days the weakness has climbed to his hands.
All reflexes are gone.
Lumbar puncture: high protein but normal cell count.
Nerve conduction: slowed (demyelination).
rounds.rev: Antibodies made against the infection (often Campylobacter) cross-react with peripheral nerve myelin. The danger is breathing muscle weakness, so lung capacity is checked often. Treatment: IV immunoglobulin or plasma exchange; most recover.
